items.title: How Dream Racers uses Roblox's Cube AI to generate playable vehicles in real time
items.excerpt: A new Roblox game, Dream Racers, integrates generative AI directly into gameplay by letting players build and race unique karts. It is one of the first shipped titles to put Roblox's Cube 3D generation model into a live player-facing loop.
items.rationale: First shipped title to make generative 3D a runtime design material rather than a pre-production asset trick — the player prompts and the game must keep it playable.

items.title: Nimble Fox launches AI tool for building Unity games worldwide
items.excerpt: A Helsinki startup is releasing an AI copilot built into the Unity editor on Sept. 7, letting developers build and modify games by prompting inside the engine. Rather than generating a whole game in one pass, it works feature by feature — mechanics, UI flows, scoped changes — reading the context of an existing project.
items.rationale: A dated, in-editor, project-aware copilot (Sept 7) — the shape AI game tooling is settling into, and something a Unity team can actually schedule around.

items.title: Nvidia says DLSS 5 comes with a 50-60% performance hit, which makes me wonder what we're doing here
items.excerpt: Nvidia has confirmed DLSS 5's 3D-guided neural rendering costs 50-60% of frame rate on average, inverting the original promise of DLSS as a performance technology.
items.rationale: The single DLSS 5 card: Nvidia's own launch numbers flip the cost model, turning a neural render pass into an explicit art-direction budget decision rather than free uplift.

items.title: Dwarf Fortress Creator Calls Out One Of AI's Biggest Issues: The Bosses Who Force Us To Use It
items.excerpt: Tarn Adams argues the real problem with generative AI in game development isn't the tools but mandated adoption: 'Everyone I know, their bosses are slowly getting psychosis.'
items.rationale: Games' most credible proceduralist moves the argument from capability to mandate — the version of the AI debate working designers actually live in.

items.title: 30 years later, I finally got to play Quake on the PS1, but that's before I found a better version that doesn't rely on "substantial AI assistance"
items.excerpt: A homebrew Quake port for PS1 was built with heavy AI coding assistance — and a rival hand-written port runs better, sparking a small but pointed comparison in the demoscene-adjacent porting community.
items.rationale: A rare controlled comparison: vibe-coded and hand-crafted versions of the same technical project shipping side by side, with measurable results.
